content: In HIV co-infected patients, a study is being conducted to evaluate treatment options and their implications. The findings will be published in a peer-reviewed journal and made available online for reference. The study's quantitative objectives include assessing stakeholders' ratings of the importance of various treatment outcomes and their perspectives on equity, feasibility, and acceptability of treatment options. The qualitative objectives aim to explore the reasons behind these ratings and views. The mixed-methods approach integrates findings from both quantitative and qualitative components. The study involved a survey of non-patient stakeholders and interviews with both patients and non-patients. Non-patient stakeholders included national officers of neglected tropical disease (NTD) programs, health ministry staff, subnational program managers, physicians, nurses, members of non-governmental organizations (NGOs), academic researchers, regional and country WHO personnel, and members of the WHO Regional Technical Advisory Group on visceral leishmaniasis (VL). The survey and interview guides were developed by guideline methodologists at the American University of Beirut, with input from the WHO secretariat. The survey was disseminated widely through WHO-recommended listservs, regional and country offices, and WHO partners, including national VL programs. Non-patient stakeholders who expressed willingness to participate in semi-structured interviews during the survey were invited for interviews. Physicians in Ethiopia and India assisted in recruiting patients for the study. The evidence-to-decision tables, available in the web annex, summarize the survey and interview results. Among the 177 survey participants, most were from South-East Asia (142 participants), followed by East Africa (32 participants). The majority were male (87%), aged 31–50 years (63%), and held advanced degrees such as doctoral (35%) or master’s degrees (36%). Stakeholder groups included health providers (36%), national NTD officers or subnational program managers (30%), researchers (11%), and NGO members (8%). Most participants were affiliated with NGOs (57%) or governmental organizations (20%). Regarding treatment outcomes, mortality was rated as the most critical outcome by 61% of participants, followed by clinical cure at six months (58%), clinical cure at treatment completion (58%), relapse (57%), serious adverse events (57%), patient satisfaction (57%), and complications (54%). Participants emphasized that clinical cure is essential for patients to resume daily life and economic productivity. Non-patient stakeholders highlighted the importance of sustained clinical cure. In terms of equity, acceptability, and feasibility, 60% of participants believed that combination therapy would increase health equity, with 40% stating it would increase and 20% stating it would probably increase equity. Combination therapy was also considered more acceptable (79%) and more feasible (57%) than monotherapy, primarily due to shorter hospitalization requirements. Longer hospital stays were viewed as less feasible and less acceptable by all participants. Semi-structured interviews revealed that both patient and non-patient stakeholders considered mortality reduction a critical outcome. Non-patient stakeholders emphasized the heightened vulnerability of co-infected and immunosuppressed patients, while patients described survival as a miracle, often recounting the loss of close relatives. Clinical cure was universally seen as an opportunity for patients to regain social and economic productivity. Non-patient stakeholders valued clinical cure at six months more than at treatment completion due to the higher risk of relapse in this population. Most participants believed that the two treatment options did not have a differential impact on equity, as both are freely available in public health facilities. However, some expressed concerns about adverse events associated with miltefosine, which makes pregnant women ineligible for combination therapy. General equity issues, such as out-of-pocket expenses in private health facilities, were also mentioned. Combination therapy was deemed more acceptable than monotherapy due to shorter hospital stays. Participants suggested several implementation considerations, including improving access to treatment, providing counseling, and adopting a holistic approach to care. Research priorities identified included disease epidemiology, diagnostics, prevention, disease progression, prognosis, treatment-related issues, immunology, the relationship with HIV, and health systems. Adverse effects of antileishmanial medicines were also documented. Miltefosine commonly causes gastrointestinal issues such as vomiting and diarrhea, with rare but severe effects like Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Paromomycin can lead to injection site pain, ototoxicity, and transient increases in liver enzymes. Liposomal amphotericin B is associated with infusion-related reactions, anemia, and renal dysfunction. Amphotericin B deoxycholate can cause severe renal and cardiac complications, while sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate are linked to cardiac arrhythmias, pancreatitis, and other systemic effects.
